quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Opinion: What a Library Is For] Whenever a council needs to cut spending, someone suggests that libraries are a relic. Books, the argument goes, are now cheaper than ever and available online. This view mistakes the library's product for its purpose. Consider who uses the Hillfield branch on a weekday morning: job seekers using the free computers to complete applications, new arrivals attending English conversation groups, parents with toddlers at story time, and older residents who come, quite simply, for company. Few of them are there for a book they could not otherwise afford. The branch is, in effect, one of the last public spaces where nobody is required to buy anything, and where staff will help with a form, a printer, or a problem. A council that measures its libraries only by the number of loans is measuring the wrong thing, much as one might judge a school by how many pencils it uses. Cuts made on that basis will save money that is later spent elsewhere, on services that struggle to reach the same people.
quests.question: What does the writer mean by saying critics mistake the library's "product" for its "purpose"?
options: Libraries exist mainly to lend books more cheaply than shops.
Libraries should be judged by the number of books they own.
Books are the visible part; libraries mainly serve as public spaces.
Libraries have never been useful to most local residents.
quests.correctAnswer: Books are the visible part; libraries mainly serve as public spaces.
quests.hint: Think about the difference between what a library hands out and what it does for people.
quests.explanation: The writer shows that most visitors come for computers, groups, story time and company, so the books are only part of what the library provides.
quests.evidenceLine: This view mistakes the library's product for its purpose

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Do Later School Start Times Help?] Several districts have moved their high school start times from 7:30 to 8:30 a.m., hoping that teenagers, whose body clocks shift later during adolescence, would sleep more and learn better. The early results are encouraging but uneven. In one district, students reported sleeping an extra 45 minutes on school nights, and first-period attendance rose by 8 percent. Another district found no change in test scores after two years, though students reported feeling less tired. Researchers note a difficulty: when school starts later, it also ends later, which can push back sports practice and part-time work, and some students simply stay up later to compensate. Parents with early work hours also face new problems, since they can no longer drop children off on their way to the office. The evidence suggests that later starts help most when they are combined with consistent bedtimes and adjusted afternoon schedules, rather than adopted on their own.
quests.question: What do the two districts' results suggest?
options: Later starts reliably raise test scores in every district.
Sleep and attendance improved, but test score gains are uncertain.
Later starts make students sleep a little less each night.
Most students prefer to return to the earlier schedules.
quests.correctAnswer: Sleep and attendance improved, but test score gains are uncertain.
quests.hint: Compare what each district measured and found.
quests.explanation: One district saw more sleep and better attendance; the other saw no change in test scores, so improvements are uneven.
quests.evidenceLine: found no change in test scores after two years

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [The Last Game] Old Mr. Petrov had played chess in the park every Sunday for as long as anyone could remember, and the young man who sat opposite him that afternoon had clearly been warned. He moved his pieces quickly, with the confidence of someone who had beaten most of the people he had ever played. Mr. Petrov said little. He lost a pawn, then a knight, and the young man began to smile. Around the board, the regulars who had gathered were strangely quiet, and a few of them were looking at their shoes. On the thirty-first move, Mr. Petrov slid a bishop across the board with two fingers, almost carelessly, and said, "I believe that is mate in three." The young man stared. He examined the board for a long minute, and when he looked up his smile was gone. "You let me take the knight," he said. Mr. Petrov shrugged. "It seemed generous."
quests.question: Why were the regulars strangely quiet and looking at their shoes?
options: They were bored with the game.
They disliked Mr. Petrov.
They were embarrassed by the young man's rudeness.
They suspected the game was not going as it seemed.
quests.correctAnswer: They suspected the game was not going as it seemed.
quests.hint: Think about why people who know Mr. Petrov would avoid watching openly.
quests.explanation: The regulars knew Mr. Petrov's reputation, so their silence suggests they expected the young man's early lead to be misleading.
quests.evidenceLine: strangely quiet

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Email to a Supplier] Dear Mr. Lindqvist, Thank you for explaining the delay to the shipment. I understand that the factory was closed for two weeks, and that this affected the first batch. However, as you know, it was the second batch that our customers were waiting for, and it is that one we need by the 20th. Your email suggests that it will arrive on the 29th, which is too late for the promotion it was intended to support. I would like to propose that you send half of it by air, at your cost, since the delay was not of our making, and that we accept the rest at the original date and price. If that is not possible, we will have to consider whether to continue ordering the product in the quantities we have until now. I would prefer to find a solution that works for us both.
quests.question: What does "that one" refer to in "it is that one we need by the 20th"?
options: The second batch
The first batch
The promotion
The factory
quests.correctAnswer: The second batch
quests.hint: Look at the noun in the previous clause that the customers were waiting for.
quests.explanation: The sentence says customers were waiting for the second batch, and "that one" refers back to it.
quests.evidenceLine: it was the second batch that our customers were waiting for

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Why Translations of Poems Differ] Ask five translators to render the same short poem, and you will receive five poems. This is not because some of them are careless. A poem is not only what it says but how it says it: the rhythm, the sounds, the associations of particular words. Translators must decide which of these to keep, because they cannot keep all of them. One may choose to preserve the literal meaning, producing a version accurate but flat. Another may aim to preserve the music, adjusting the words to keep the rhythm, at the cost of precision. A third may try to recreate the effect on the reader, which can mean changing an image to one that carries the same feeling in the new language. None of these approaches is simply wrong. Readers who want to understand a poem should, if possible, read two or three translations side by side, since the differences between them reveal what the original contains.
quests.question: Why do translations of the same poem differ?
options: Some translators are careless and rush their work to meet deadlines.
Poems are too simple for any two translators to agree about.
Languages share the same words, so differences are just chance.
Translators must choose what to keep, since they cannot keep everything.
quests.correctAnswer: Translators must choose what to keep, since they cannot keep everything.
quests.hint: The passage says the differences are "not because" of carelessness.
quests.explanation: A poem has meaning, rhythm, sound and association, and a translator cannot preserve them all.
quests.evidenceLine: they cannot keep all of them

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [The Summer the Thames Smelled] In the summer of 1858, London's river became unbearable. For years the city had been pouring sewage into the Thames, and an unusually hot, dry season turned the water into a slow-moving mass of waste. The smell was so strong that Parliament, which sits beside the river, hung curtains soaked in chemicals at its windows and considered moving elsewhere. Doctors had long argued that disease was spread by foul air, so the smell frightened politicians in a way that arguments about water quality had not. Within weeks, a bill authorizing a new system of sewers passed with unusual speed. The engineer Joseph Bazalgette built a network that carried waste downstream and away from the center, and the cholera outbreaks that had killed thousands in earlier decades stopped. Ironically, the theory that persuaded politicians to act, that bad air carried disease, was wrong; the real danger had been the contaminated water. Yet the reform worked anyway.
quests.question: Why did the smell prompt action when earlier arguments had not?
options: The river had never before smelled bad, which shocked the city's leaders.
Politicians were persuaded by detailed engineers' drawings of new sewers.
It matched a belief that foul air spread disease, which alarmed politicians.
It forced the city to move Parliament away from the river for good.
quests.correctAnswer: It matched a belief that foul air spread disease, which alarmed politicians.
quests.hint: Link the doctors' belief to the politicians' fear.
quests.explanation: Doctors had said foul air spread disease, so a terrible smell frightened politicians in a way arguments about water quality had not.
quests.evidenceLine: so the smell frightened politicians in a way that arguments about water quality had not

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Two Ways to Run a Meeting] At Marlow Design, weekly meetings once ran for ninety minutes, with each person reporting on their projects in turn. Attendance was high, and so was irritation. Last year the director replaced them with a different format: a one-page summary is circulated the evening before, the meeting lasts thirty minutes, and it is spent only on decisions and disagreements. Supporters say the change saves each employee about an hour a week and forces people to prepare. A staff survey after six months showed opinion divided almost evenly. Critics point out that the new meeting is less social; the old format, however tedious, kept people informed about each other's work and gave quieter colleagues a chance to speak. The director concedes the loss and has introduced a monthly lunch, on the grounds that it is better to be honest about the purpose of a gathering than to disguise a social need as a status update.
quests.question: How does the new format differ from the old one?
options: It is longer and more social, with each person speaking in turn.
It requires every person to report on their own projects in turn.
It takes place every day so that decisions are made faster.
It is shorter and focuses on decisions after a summary is circulated.
quests.correctAnswer: It is shorter and focuses on decisions after a summary is circulated.
quests.hint: Compare length, preparation and content of the two formats.
quests.explanation: The old meeting lasted ninety minutes with reports from everyone; the new one lasts thirty minutes and covers only decisions, based on a summary read beforehand.
quests.evidenceLine: a one-page summary is circulated the evening before

quests.passage: [An Ordinary Kindness] The bus was late, the rain was heavy, and I had just received an email that made my week harder. When I finally boarded, I took the last free seat, folded my wet umbrella onto my lap, and stared at nothing. At the next stop, an elderly man climbed on, looked around, and began to make his way toward the back, gripping the handrails. I considered standing. I did not. I was tired, I told myself, and he looked more capable than he moved. A teenage girl across the aisle got up without a word and gestured to her seat. He thanked her warmly. "It's nothing," she said, and went back to her phone. I have not forgotten the moment. Nothing happened to me; I did nothing wrong, exactly. But I keep returning to how easily I had arranged my reasons, and how little they weighed against her quiet standing.
quests.question: What is the writer's attitude toward their own behavior?
options: Proud and satisfied
Uncomfortable and self-critical
Indifferent to what happened
Angry at the teenage girl
quests.correctAnswer: Uncomfortable and self-critical
quests.hint: Notice the "But" near the end and what the writer keeps returning to.
quests.explanation: The writer says nothing was exactly wrong yet keeps thinking about how easily excuses were made, which shows discomfort with their own inaction.
quests.evidenceLine: how easily I had arranged my reasons

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [School Cafeteria Audit: Food Waste] An audit of five school cafeterias found that students throw away an average of 28 percent of the food they are served. Fruit and vegetables account for the largest share by weight, and waste is highest in the meal served immediately before recess, when students are eager to leave. Cafeterias that moved recess to before lunch saw waste fall by about a third. Students interviewed said they prefer to eat after playing, because they feel hungrier. The report suggests that this single scheduling change does more than redesigning menus, although healthier menus are worth pursuing on other grounds. It cautions against drawing broad conclusions: three of the five schools shared a district, and one school changed its supplier during the audit, which may have affected the results. The authors recommend a larger study before any district-wide changes are made, but note that moving recess costs almost nothing and can be tested immediately.
quests.question: What is the audit's main finding about the timing of recess?
options: Moving recess before lunch reduced waste by about a third.
Longer recess periods reduced waste by about a third.
Waste was lowest in the meal that was served just before recess.
Menu redesign was the most important factor in reducing waste.
quests.correctAnswer: Moving recess before lunch reduced waste by about a third.
quests.hint: Look for the result of changing the order of recess and lunch.
quests.explanation: Cafeterias that held recess before lunch saw about a third less waste.
quests.evidenceLine: Cafeterias that moved recess to before lunch saw waste fall by about a third

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Letter of Resignation] Dear Ms. Alder, Please accept this letter as formal notice of my resignation from the post of operations coordinator, effective 30 November. I have valued my four years with the company and the colleagues with whom I have worked, many of whom I count as friends. I am grateful for the opportunities I have had, particularly the chance to lead the warehouse relocation. I would, however, like to be frank about one matter. Over the past year, my role has expanded considerably, and while my responsibilities have grown, my title and salary have not. I raised this on two occasions and was told that the matter would be reviewed. I understand that budgets are limited, and I do not write this to apportion blame. I mention it only because I would not want my successor to be told the same. I will do everything I can to ensure a smooth handover before I leave.
quests.question: What reason for resigning does the letter imply?
options: A long-running conflict with several colleagues at work
Growth in duties without a matching change in title or pay
A wish to retire early and spend more time at home
Dissatisfaction with the way the warehouse move was run
quests.correctAnswer: Growth in duties without a matching change in title or pay
quests.hint: Read the paragraph that begins "I would, however, like to be frank".
quests.explanation: The writer says responsibilities have grown while title and salary have not, and raising it twice led nowhere.
quests.evidenceLine: my responsibilities have grown, my title and salary have not
